headline: Blinkist halts AI narration after 2 years, citing lack of 'depth' and 'human connection'
summary: After extensive testing, Blinkist concluded AI narration couldn't deliver the same depth, spark curiosity, or make information stick as human narrators. This decision reflects a growing trend of companies re-evaluating AI's real-world impact.
details: Blinkist, a pioneer in audio learning, officially announced on June 14, 2026, that it is discontinuing AI narration. After two years of extensive testing and refinement, the company concluded that AI could not match the quality of human narrators.

Thomas Anderson, VP of Content at Blinkist, stated that no AI narration, "no matter how polished, can deliver the same depth that a human narrator can." He emphasized that human narrators are experts in sharing insights in ways that spark curiosity and ensure information retention.

This move comes amidst a broader trend in 2026 where the initial hype around AI is colliding with practical realities. Despite global AI capital expenditure projected at $527 billion, many organizations are quietly scaling back AI implementations that fail to deliver expected results.

Blinkist found that while AI voice generation can sound human, it lacks the ability to interpret, emphasize, or bring an author's personality to life. These are emotional and artistic problems that cannot be solved solely with more training data.

The company's decision highlights the difference between AI being "good enough" and truly "good," especially for a product focused on learning retention. For Blinkist, the 10% gap in quality between AI and human narration was critical.

Blinkist is not abandoning AI entirely; they continue to offer "Blinkist AI" as a Pro feature for summarizing articles, PDFs, and videos. This approach uses AI for mechanical tasks like extraction and organization, while humans handle the artistry of narration and emotional connection.

The company's reversal offers key lessons for AI product builders: measure what users truly value, avoid the "good enough" trap, and prioritize honesty to build trust. Blinkist chose product quality over cost savings by admitting AI's limitations in this specific use case.

headline: Enjoy programming in the age of AI by letting agents code in simpler languages
summary: As AI writes more code, developers can reclaim enjoyment by guiding AI to use simpler, English-like languages, shifting focus from writing complex code to validating and evolving the language itself.
details: It's widely accepted that as AI writes more and more of our code, opportunities decrease for newcomers to gain the skills needed to become professional programmers. Experienced developers also bemoan losing skills they worked hard to gain. Programming, a blend of science and art, offers deep satisfaction from capturing knowledge and applying creativity, but AI is perceived as depriving us of these opportunities.

The author, Graham Trott, has been using agentic AI like Copilot and Claude Code for about a year. Initially, he found Copilot made mistakes and produced repetitive code. A major challenge was validating the vast amounts of complex JS or Python code generated, especially as he wasn't a first-class programmer himself.

A key insight emerged: modern, high-level languages like JS or Python are too complex for AI. They suffer from inconsistencies and outdated documentation, and their many 'guardrails' designed to prevent human errors actually make AI's job harder, as AI doesn't make the same mistakes.

This led to an obvious path: if the AI agent was trying to write code in a simpler language, why not let it? Trott built an AGENT.md file instructing the AI to code in his English-like scripting language, AllSpeak, providing links to its repository and documentation.

The benefits were immediate. Instead of sifting through complex JS and Python, the application was built in a language much closer to English. Furthermore, the AI began suggesting new, syntactically valid constructs for AllSpeak, effectively evolving the language itself.

This approach transforms the human's role from writing complex code to reading and validating it. Because AllSpeak is close to English, new syntax meanings are easily understood. The language can grow in complexity while maintaining human readability, making the process more enjoyable and collaborative with AI.
